WinPrep 0.2.0-alpha.2 fixes Audit Mode detection, which did not work on any
real Windows installation. The previous build queried a registry value name
that real Windows never writes and required a setup command line that real
systems never carry, so every machine - including genuine Audit Mode
machines - was rejected as "setup state unknown", blocking both operations.

## What was wrong

Two independent defects, either of which alone broke detection:

1. The detector read `StateName` from
   `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Setup\State`. That name
   appears in the prose of Microsoft's "Windows Setup States" documentation,
   but the page's own examples - and every real installation, deployment
   script, and field report - use `ImageState`. No `StateName` value has
   ever been observed on a real machine, so the read always came back
   empty.
2. The detector required `HKLM\SYSTEM\Setup\CmdLine` to equal `audit.exe`.
   On real systems that value holds whatever the setup engine queued before
   logon - `oobe\windeploy.exe`, `SetupComplete.cmd`, or nothing - so the
   required combination could never occur.

## How detection works now

WinPrep reads the setup state from `ImageState` (with `State.ini` and the
documented `StateName` name as fallbacks), the audit boot flag under
`HKLM\SYSTEM\Setup\Status` (`AuditBoot` and its Windows 11-observed
`AuditBootVolatile` sibling), the OOBE indicator, and the session user's
SID. Audit Mode is confirmed only when the signals agree; anything missing
or contradictory stays "uncertain", and uncertain machines get no
state-changing operations. `CmdLine` is reported as an observation only.

The new `winprep signals` command prints every raw value the detector read,
where it came from, and how the state was evaluated - the evidence to attach
if a genuine Audit Mode session is ever rejected. See
docs/troubleshooting.md for the full procedure.

## Also fixed in this release

- The handover fails closed when the process list cannot be read, and the
  full preflight re-runs after confirmation, so a blocker that appears in
  the meantime (a new account, a pending restart) stops the handover before
  anything is deleted.
- The cleanup refuses to traverse an approved directory that became a
  symlink or junction after planning, closing a redirection attack window.
- A failed cleanup can be retried in the same window; the operation lock is
  released unless the reseal was initiated.
- The TUI confirmation screen shows the cleanup plan it is asking about,
  and several smaller TUI defects (stale notices, cancelled status check,
  Ctrl+C falling into the fallback menu) are fixed.
- Running WinPrep no longer creates `%ProgramData%\WinPrep` on inspection
  alone, so dry runs are strictly read-only.

## Verification status

- Unit tests (fakes) and cross-platform checks pass on Linux; Windows
  integration tests run in CI on a normally deployed Windows runner, which
  must be classified as a deployed installation. The integration suite now
  asserts that `ImageState` is actually read - the regression guard for
  defect 1.
- A regression test reproducing the real-world Audit Mode machine (the
  registry shape observed in field reports: `ImageState` set, `AuditBoot`
  set, no `StateName`, no `audit.exe` command line, built-in Administrator
  session) fails against the previous implementation and passes now.
- What has NOT been verified: a live Windows Audit Mode session. This
  release was developed without access to a real Audit Mode machine, so the
  signal set is grounded in Microsoft's documentation, production deployment
  tooling, and field reports (Windows 7-10 audit machines). In particular
  the audit boot flag is not officially documented by Microsoft. A machine
  that is genuinely in Audit Mode but lacks the expected signals is
  reported as uncertain with its reasons - never guessed - and
  `winprep signals` produces exactly the evidence needed to extend the
  rules.
- The full Windows lifecycle (real handover and verified OOBE boot) remains
  unexecuted, which is why this is still a prerelease.

## Upgrading

Replace `winprep.exe`. No configuration, manifest format, or command changes
affect existing usage; `winprep signals` is new.
